title: Fabric Finishes
summary: A finish is a treatment given to a fabric to change its appearance, handling (touch) or performance and make it more suitable for its end use. A fabric given a finish is a finished textile. Gray goods (unfinished textiles) come directly from the loom, are dull, wrinkled and uneven, have little customer appeal and are used for rough work, backing or packaging; they are not actually gray in colour. Finishes improve appearance, give variety through dyeing and printing, improve feel, make fabric more useful, improve the draping of light fabrics and suit an end use.

By function: basic (aesthetic) finishes applied to almost all fabrics – scouring, bleaching, starching, calendering, and also dyeing and printing; functional or special finishes for a specific purpose – fire-proof, waterproof, bullet-proof, crease-resistant. By degree of performance: temporary (run off in the first wash, e.g. starching), semi-durable (last several washes, e.g. bleaching), durable (last the life of the fabric, e.g. permanent pleats, wrinkle-resistant), permanent (chemical treatment changes the fibre, e.g. waterproofing, fire-proofing). By process: chemical (wet) finishes – durable or permanent, e.g. fire-proof, crease-resistant; mechanical (dry) finishes – moisture, pressure, heat or a device, e.g. beating, brushing, calendering – temporary or semi-durable.

Scouring (cleaning): industrial washing of fabric with warm water and soap solution to remove oils, starches and waxes; it cleans the fabric and makes it more absorbent (cotton is boiled in soap solution, silk is boiled to remove gum – degumming, wool is boiled to remove grease). Bleaching: a chemical treatment to remove paleness or colour and make fibre, yarn or fabric white; hydrogen peroxide for protein fibres (silk, wool) and sodium hypochlorite for cotton; man-made fibres need none; strong bleach damages fabric. Starching (stiffening): makes fabric heavier, stiff, crisp, shiny and smooth (muslin, poplin, cambric, thin silks); loosely woven fabric starched heavily shows its weave after the first wash. Calendering: industrial ironing – the fabric passes through smooth hot rollers to remove wrinkles and give a smooth, lustrous look.

Pre-shrinking (sanforisation) prevents shrinkage after washing (labels: sanforised, anti-shrink, shrink-proof). Mercerisation: cotton is treated with sodium hydroxide to make it strong, lustrous and absorbent and to improve dye uptake (routine for cotton; sewing threads are mercerised). Parchmentisation: cotton is treated with a mild acid that partly eats away the fabric, giving permanently stiff, transparent, light organdy that needs no starch. Wash 'n' wear: cotton, linen or wool treated so that it does not wrinkle much and can be worn without or with little ironing. Dyeing gives solid colour; printing applies colour only to selected areas to make designs; the colour should be colourfast.
## Dyes, stages of dyeing, decorative dyeing and printing

Natural dyes (turmeric, henna, madder, indigo from plants; tyrian purple and lac from animals; khaki from minerals) are eco-friendly but slow, difficult and expensive. Synthetic dyes (direct, basic, acid, disperse, azo, vat, reactive) are easy to use, brighter and faster but polluting and may cause allergies; azo dyes are banned. Textiles are dyed at the fibre stage (popular for man-made fibres, uniform and fast, but wastage), yarn stage (knitting yarn, threads), fabric stage (most dyeing; uniform; good for blends) and garment stage (piece dyeing; no fabric wastage but colour may be uneven near seams).

Resist (decorative) dyeing uses a resist to keep dye from selected areas. Tie and dye uses thread: marbling, binding, knotting, folding, peg tying, tritik; Patola of Gujarat is tied and dyed in the yarn before weaving, bandhani of Rajasthan in the woven fabric. Batik uses wax (beeswax and paraffin wax) as the resist, removed later. Printing methods: block, screen, roller, stencil; in block printing a wooden block with an engraved design is pressed into thick dye paste and stamped on the fabric (Sanganer, Jaipur); at home vegetables such as ladies' finger or onion can be used as blocks.

State True or False: (i) A chemical finish is also known as a wet finish. (ii) A permanent finish is given by chemical treatment. (iii) Wool fabrics are cleaned to remove gum. (iv) Scouring is done with a mixture of water and soap.
(i) True. (ii) True. (iii) False – wool is cleaned to remove grease and oils; gum is removed from silk. (iv) True.

State True or False: (i) Marbling is a technique of tie and dye. (ii) Yarn is dyed before weaving in Patola. (iii) Thread is used as a resist material in batik. (iv) Block printing can be done at home with vegetables.
(i) True. (ii) True. (iii) False – wax is the resist in batik; thread is used in tie and dye. (iv) True.

The fibre stage, the yarn stage, the fabric stage and the garment (piece) stage.

Briefly explain the batik method of resist dyeing.

In batik wax (a mixture of beeswax and paraffin wax) is applied with a brush or block on selected areas of the fabric as a resist; when the fabric is dyed, these areas do not take colour, and the wax is later removed, leaving a pattern.

Classify finishes on the basis of their functions and give two examples of each.

Basic (aesthetic) finishes – scouring, bleaching, starching, calendering, applied to almost all fabrics. Functional (special) finishes – fire-proof and waterproof, bullet-proof and crease-resistant finishes for a specific purpose.

Differentiate between dyeing and printing.

Dyeing gives a solid colour to the whole fabric (at fibre, yarn or fabric stage); printing applies colour to selected areas of the fabric surface only to make designs, so it is called selective dyeing.
Why is a mercerised fabric preferred? Give two advantages.
Mercerisation with sodium hydroxide makes cotton strong, lustrous and absorbent, and it improves dye uptake; sewing threads are mercerised too.
What is a gray fabric? Why do customers not prefer it?
A fabric that comes directly from the loom with no finish. It looks dull, wrinkled and uneven, so it lacks customer appeal and is used for backing and packaging.
State two differences between natural and synthetic dyes.

Natural dyes come from plants, animals or minerals, are eco-friendly but slow, difficult and expensive to use; synthetic dyes are made from chemicals, are easy to use, brighter and faster but pollute and may cause allergies.
sa: Classify finishes on the basis of degree of performance with one example each.

Temporary finishes run off in the first wash, e.g. starching. Semi-durable finishes stay for several washes, e.g. bleaching and certain dyes. Durable finishes last through the life of the fabric but may lose effect after many washes, e.g. permanent pleats and wrinkle-resistance. Permanent finishes are given by chemical treatment that changes the fibre structure and stay for life, e.g. waterproofing and fire-proofing.

Scouring is the industrial cleaning of fabric with warm water and soap solution to remove oils, starch and wax added for weaving; it makes the fabric clean and more absorbent. Bleaching is a chemical treatment that removes colour or paleness and makes fabric white so that light shades of dye come out well; hydrogen peroxide is used for silk and wool and sodium hypochlorite for cotton; strong bleach can harm the fabric.
Explain the tie and dye techniques with examples.

Thread is used as a resist to keep dye from selected areas. Marbling: the fabric is crumpled into a ball and tied at random. Binding: the fabric is picked up at points and tied at intervals. Knotting: knots are put where wanted. Folding: pleated and folded fabric is tied at intervals for lines. Peg tying: pegs or clamps are used. Patola (Gujarat) is tied and dyed in the yarn before weaving; bandhani (Rajasthan) is tied and dyed in woven fabric.
la: Describe pre-shrinking, mercerisation, parchmentisation, wash 'n' wear and calendering in a sentence each, and name one use.

Pre-shrinking (sanforisation) prevents further shrinkage in washing. Mercerisation treats cotton with sodium hydroxide to make it strong, lustrous and absorbent. Parchmentisation treats cotton with mild acid to make stiff, transparent organdy. Wash 'n' wear gives cotton, linen or wool a crease-resistant finish that needs little or no ironing (for uniforms). Calendering passes fabric through hot rollers to remove wrinkles and add lustre.
Explain the importance of textile finishes and the stages of dyeing in five points each (briefly).

Importance: improve appearance; give variety through dyeing and printing; improve the feel of the fabric; make it more useful; improve the draping of light fabrics; make it suitable for its end use. Stages of dyeing: fibre (uniform and fast, popular for man-made fibres, but wastage); yarn (knitting yarn and threads); fabric (most dyeing, uniform, suits blends); garment (no fabric wastage, but uneven near seams).
